title: The Burning Bush and the Name of God
summary: While shepherding his father-in-law's flock near Horeb, the mountain of God, Moses sees a bush that burns without burning up. God calls to him from the bush, tells him he is on holy ground, and announces that he has seen his people's affliction and has come down to rescue them, sending Moses to Pharaoh. When Moses protests, God promises his presence, reveals his name, I AM WHO I AM, the LORD, and foretells Pharaoh's resistance, God's mighty acts, and Israel's departure with the wealth of Egypt.
story: At the end of Exodus 2 God heard Israel's groaning and remembered his covenant. This chapter is the answer. Moses, once a prince of Egypt and now a shepherd in the wilderness, meets the God of his ancestors at the mountain where Israel will later receive the covenant. God introduces himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, tying this new rescue to the promises of Genesis, and then lays out the plan of the whole book: Moses will go to Pharaoh, Pharaoh will refuse, God will strike Egypt with wonders, and the people will come out and worship God on this very mountain (v. 12). The promise of a land flowing with milk and honey looks further ahead to the conquest. Moses' reluctance, which begins here with “Who am I?”, continues through Exodus 4 before he finally returns to Egypt.
historical:
Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, whose location is debated. Christian tradition since late antiquity has placed it at Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, while others propose sites in the northern Sinai or in northwest Arabia, the land of Midian, where Moses had been living. It is called the mountain of God here perhaps because of what it would become for Israel, though some think it was already regarded as a sacred mountain. Moses' father-in-law, the priest of Midian, is now called Jethro (see the note on Exodus 2).

The peoples listed in verses 8 and 17, Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, are a standard biblical list of the inhabitants of Canaan. The Hittites named here are probably groups in Canaan known by that name, as in Genesis 23, rather than the great Hittite empire of Anatolia. The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David took it. The phrase a land flowing with milk and honey describes rich pasture for goats and sheep and abundant sweetness, whether from bees or from fruit syrup; an Egyptian text, the Story of Sinuhe, similarly praises a region of Canaan for its honey, figs, grapes, and oil.
cultural:
Taking off one's sandals was a sign of reverence and humility, as when Joshua was told to do the same before the commander of the LORD's army (Joshua 5:15). The ground was holy not because of the place but because of the presence there. Hiding one's face before God (v. 6) reflects the belief, stated in Exodus 33:20, that no one can see God's face and live.

In the ancient world a name expressed character and made a relationship possible, which is why Moses asks what he should say when the people ask God's name. They knew the God of their fathers; the question is what this God will prove to be for them now. The elders of Israel (v. 16) were the heads of families and clans who represented the people. The request to Pharaoh for a three-day trip into the wilderness to sacrifice (v. 18) was a familiar kind of request. Absence records from the Egyptian workmen's village at Deir el-Medina list making an offering to a god among the reasons for missing work.
literary: The chapter follows a pattern found in several biblical call stories: God appears, speaks, commissions, meets an objection with reassurance, and gives a sign. The same pattern shapes the calls of Gideon (Judges 6) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1). The verb see drives the opening. Moses turns aside to see the great sight, the LORD sees that he has turned aside, and God says, literally, I have surely seen the affliction of my people (v. 7). God's speech in verses 7 to 10 is a string of first-person verbs: I have seen, I have heard, I know, I have come down to rescue, and then, surprisingly, “I am sending you.” Moses' first objection, “Who am I?”, is answered not with praise of Moses but with God's presence: “I will surely be with you.” In Hebrew that promise begins with the same verb form, ehyeh, that God then uses for his name in verse 14. The bush (seneh) may also be a play on the name Sinai, and the fire in the bush anticipates the fire on the mountain in Exodus 19.

outline.t: The bush that burns and is not consumed
God has seen his people's affliction and sends Moses
“Who am I?” and the promise of God's presence
Instructions for the elders and Pharaoh, and what will follow

doctrines.note: God reveals himself as I AM WHO I AM and as the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The name speaks of a God who is not defined or limited by anything outside himself, who is present and faithful, and who will show who he is by what he does. The church has long read the name as pointing to God's self-existence and unchanging faithfulness.

The bush burns without being consumed, and the ground around it becomes holy. Holiness is God's own set-apart, blazing purity, and it makes the ordinary places he enters holy. It is dangerous to approach carelessly, yet this holy God speaks and comes near to rescue.

“I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians” (v. 8). Salvation in Exodus starts with God's initiative, moved by his people's suffering and his covenant promises. It is rescue from a real oppressor into a real place, and its goal is worship: the people are brought out to serve God on his mountain.

words.note: Hayah, to be, to become, to happen. God's name in verse 14 is built from this verb: ehyeh asher ehyeh, rendered I AM WHO I AM, which can also be translated I will be what I will be. The same form, ehyeh, appears in verse 12: I will be with you. The name is not an abstract definition but a promise of presence. Interpreters debate whether its main sense is God's self-existence, his freedom, or his faithful presence; the Hebrew can carry all three.

YHWH, the personal name of God, usually printed as LORD in small capitals in English Bibles. It is related to the verb to be in verse 14. Out of reverence, Jews stopped pronouncing the name in the centuries before Christ and said Adonai (Lord) instead, and its original pronunciation is uncertain; scholars commonly reconstruct it as Yahweh. God calls it “My name forever” (v. 15).

Qodesh, holiness, the quality of belonging to God and being set apart from the common. The ground is holy ground (v. 5) because God is present. This is the first time the word is used of a place in the Bible, and Exodus will go on to build a whole system of holy space, holy objects, and holy people around God's presence in the tabernacle.

Natsal, to rescue, snatch away, or strip. God has come down to rescue his people (v. 8), and the same verb, in another form, describes Israel plundering the Egyptians (v. 22). The one act strips Egypt of both its slaves and its wealth.

christ: Jesus himself uses this chapter. When the Sadducees denied the resurrection, he pointed to the passage about the bush, where God says he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and concluded that God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26-27). In John's Gospel Jesus says that before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), and his hearers pick up stones, apparently hearing a claim to the name revealed here; the Septuagint had rendered verse 14 with the Greek words for I am. Many early Christian writers also read the angel of the LORD in the bush as an appearance of the Son before his incarnation, though others take the angel as a messenger speaking in God's name. Most of all, the pattern of the chapter, the God who sees his people's suffering and comes down to rescue them, is the pattern the New Testament finds fulfilled when the Son came down from heaven to save.

hard.q: Did God tell Moses to deceive Pharaoh about a three-day trip, and to take Egypt's wealth?
hard.a:
God tells Moses to ask Pharaoh for a three-day trip into the wilderness to sacrifice (v. 18), though the plan is for Israel to leave for good. Some readers see this as a deliberately modest first request, a test that exposes Pharaoh's hardness; God says in the next verse that Pharaoh will refuse even this. The request never promises a return, and as the plagues unfold the full demand becomes plain to Pharaoh (for example 10:8-11). Others acknowledge that the request conceals the full plan and judge it as a legitimate strategy against a tyrant who has already ordered the murder of Israel's children, comparable to the midwives' answer in chapter 1.

As for the silver and gold, the Hebrew verb in verse 22 means to ask, not to borrow, as some older translations rendered it. The Egyptians give because God grants the people favor (v. 21; 12:35-36). Readers have long seen this as wages for generations of unpaid labor and as the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham that his descendants would come out with great possessions (Genesis 15:14). Israel's later law made the same point: a freed slave was not to be sent away empty-handed (Deuteronomy 15:13-14). The same gold will be used for both the golden calf and the tabernacle, and Exodus leaves the reader to notice what a freed people does with its wealth.

questions: Moses asked, “Who am I?” and God answered with a promise about himself: “I will surely be with you.” What changes when the question shifts from your own adequacy to God's presence?
God says he has seen, heard, and knows the suffering of his people, and has come down. Where do you most need to hear that God sees your situation?
Moses had to turn aside to look at the bush before God spoke. What would it look like for you to slow down and pay attention to where God may be speaking?
